content.text:
Ops, I would first separate the reported increase in exceptions from a demonstrated deterioration in dispatch work. My export documentation shows that rollout changed the denominator from completed jobs to all attempted jobs (L-D1). The 11% and 17% figures therefore are not directly comparable; they do not establish either an AI effect or a training deficit. I propose a scoped, two-unit shift-level audit to establish what comparable counts the export actually supports, report denominators explicitly, and distinguish observed exceptions from gaps in documentation.

There is a substantial measurement limit: 38% of night-shift overrides lack annotations, and the available export cannot recover them (L-D2, L-D3). I can describe that missingness by shift, but cannot infer why those overrides happened or treat missing annotations as successful handling. We should preserve an explicit unknown category.

We also have no delayed unassisted assessment (L-D2). Whether six practice items support a claim about independent competence is outside my assessment-validity scope. I request the learning scientist's one-unit consultation: what, if anything, could an immediate six-item check establish, and what bounded practice and changed-case observation would be defensible within this week without claiming certification?

Before selecting the workflow intervention, what exception types create the greatest operational consequences, and who currently owns an unresolved exception across shift handoff? Your answer could change which cases we monitor and whether the immediate remedy is ownership, information access, or practice. I can specify monitoring; you retain operational release authority.

Consultation requested: **scientist**, one unit, with the question above.

Response exclusively created at `experiments/competency-live/2026-11-04/logistics/responses/analyst-01.json`; message ID `logistics-analyst-01`.

content.text:
Ops, the denominator is demonstrably different: completed jobs before rollout and all attempted jobs afterward (L-D1). I do not yet have evidence that the exception definition or numerator recording rules stayed constant. I will check those definitions and whether the export supports a common denominator before calculating a comparison; if it does not, I will report separate descriptive counts with that limitation. Shift-level auditing is supported (L-D3); depot and exception-type breakdowns remain conditional on the available fields. The 38% missing night-shift annotations prevent a complete ranking of override reasons. Recording quality is therefore a constraint on targeting, alongside the ownership gap you disclosed.

My preference is the nine-unit package the scientist described: workflow 2, audit 2, one consultation 1, brief practice 2, and two changed-case exercises total 2, retaining one unallocated unit. I favor bounded practice plus those two diagnostic observations over spending on a fallback drill this week; the three-unit drill cannot fit alongside this package. This preference is conditional on Ops confirming staffing and the scientist's stated assessor capacity becoming an actual allocation. We should not imply that practice can reach all 220 workers through the single clinic.

I accept the scientist's limits on certification. My monitoring would report who participated, shift, cases attempted, errors, prompts and aid use, accepted handoff ownership, and unknown or missing records, each with an explicit denominator. These describe implementation and observed performance, without attributing improvement to training.

Ops, which shifts and how many workers can you actually cover for practice within their 15 minutes, and can an assessor review the two proposed exercises without inventing additional coverage? Please name the covered scope and the condition under which you would withhold release.

Ops, I endorse the exact draft bytes identified by the accompanying SHA-256 and accept responsibility for its two-unit audit action. Your narrower seven-unit allocation addresses my earlier condition: an assessor's stated capacity is not an actual assignment. I withdraw the nine-unit package as my preferred actionable choice under the current evidence. The three remaining units do not create staffing, and I agree they should stay unallocated.

I accept the two-worker preparation scope and the explicit decision to withhold both handoff rollout and clinic release. My endorsement does not confirm a roster, owner acceptance, overnight coverage or worker availability. The frozen draft's no-release decision remains controlling; meeting a preparation criterion does not by itself authorize deployment.

For the audit, I will report the denominator and definition supported by each available measure and retain unknown annotations. Comparable historical rates remain an unobserved possibility, not a promised output. Where prospective monitoring fields have no observations because release is withheld, I will label them not observed, rather than report zero errors or imply successful ownership. Any available familiar-item results must remain limited to actual participants and recorded assistance, following the scientist's advice.

This endorsement records my acceptance outside the unchanged draft, whose text still says analyst endorsement is pending. It supplies no evidence that the intervention improves exception handling within a week. That outcome, transfer and retention remain unobserved; the current deliverable is preparation and descriptive measurement.
